parole.significato: A summons to arms, as on the approach of an enemy.
parole.testo: From Middle English alarme, alarom, borrowed from Middle French alarme, itself from Old Italian all'arme! (“to arms!, to the weapons!”), ultimately from Latin arma (“arms, weapons”).

parole.significato: Any measure of central tendency, especially any mean, the median, or the mode.
parole.testo: Not entirely certain. The oldest meaning in English is “customs duty”. parole.significato: The act or state of declining or sinking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cadence, from Old Italian cadenza (“conclusion of a phrase of music”), from Latin *cadentia (literally “a falling”), form of cadēns, the present participle of cadō (“to fall, to cease”). The Latin verb is inherited, via Proto-Italic *kadō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱad-e-

parole.significato: Lacking the proper care or concern for something important, reckless, rash, high-handed.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1562 in a translation by Peter Whitehorne. parole.significato: A mountebank, someone who addresses crowds in the street; (especially), an itinerant seller of medicines or drugs.
parole.testo: From Middle French charlatan, from Old Italian ciarlatano (“quack”), a blend of ciarlatore (“chatterer”) + cerretano (“hawker, quack”, literally “native of Cerreto”) (Cerreto di Spoleto being a village in Umbria, known for its quacks).

parole.significato: A gold coin minted by various European nations.
parole.testo: From Middle French ducat, late Old French ducat, from Old Italian ducato, from Medieval Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of dux (“duke; leader”). Doublet of duchy.

parole.significato: The function or duty of an ambassador.
parole.testo: Modern variant of obsolete ambassy, from Middle French ambassee (“mission, embassy”), from Old French ambascee (also enbassee (“message for a high official, official mission”)) from Old Italian ambasciata, from Old Occitan ambaissada (“embassy”), derived from ambaissa (“message”), from Late Latin am

parole.significato: To have luster, to gleam, to shine.
parole.testo: From Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro, from Old Italian lustrare (“brighten”), from Latin lūstrō (“to purify, to brighten”), from Latin lūstrum (“purification ritual”).

parole.significato: A person who poses as a subject or visual reference for an artist.
parole.testo: From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.

parole.significato: A person of preeminent qualities, who acts as a pattern or model for others.

First attested in the 1570s from Middle French sentinelle (“watch or guard kept by a soldier”), from Old Italian sentinella, probably from sentina + -ella, from sentire (“perceive, watch, hear”), from sentiō (“feel, perceive by the senses”). See also sense, sentient.

parole.significato: A small flat-bottomed open boat with a pointed bow and square stern.
parole.testo: From Middle English skif, from Middle French esquif, from Old Italian schifo (“small boat”), from Lombardic skif (“boat”), from Proto-Germanic *skipą (“boat, ship”). Doublet of ship.
